content: Capillary malformations (CM) are simple vascular malformations that can present with a wide range of clinical manifestations. They may occur as isolated anomalies, in combination with other vascular anomalies such as lymphatic or venous malformations, or as part of multi-system syndromes. The diagnosis and management of CM depend on their clinical presentation, histopathological behavior, and any coexisting anomalies. Nevus Simplex Nevus simplex, also known as salmon patch, angel kiss, or stork bite, is a common vascular anomaly seen in newborns. It appears as single or multiple blanchable, pink-red patches with poorly defined borders. These lesions are asymptomatic and are often located on the nape of the neck, the forehead between the eyebrows, or the eyelids. They may become more noticeable during crying or temperature changes. Most lesions fade within one to two years, although some may persist on the back of the neck. No treatment is typically required unless requested by the patient. However, imaging studies are recommended if a lumbosacral nevus simplex is associated with other lumbosacral abnormalities, such as a dermal sinus, pit, lipoma, patch of hypertrichosis, or a deviated gluteal cleft, to evaluate for underlying spinal dysraphism. Cutaneous and/or Mucosal Capillary Malformations (Port-Wine Stain) Port-wine stains are vascular malformations of developmental origin, characterized pathologically by ectasia of superficial dermal capillaries and clinically by persistent macular erythema. These lesions are most commonly found on the face and can range in color from pale pink to deep red or purple. They vary in size from a few millimeters to several centimeters in diameter. Port-wine stains are typically flat, non-painful, and do not regress spontaneously. Port-wine stains can be classified into: Non-syndromic CM CM with central nervous system (CNS) and/or ocular anomalies (e.g., Sturge-Weber syndrome) CM with bone and/or soft tissue overgrowth Diffuse CM with overgrowth (DCMO) Most port-wine stains are sporadic and caused by somatic mutations in the GNAQ or GNA11 genes, with the Arg183Gln mutation being the most common. Some lesions are associated with other abnormalities, such as glaucoma, soft tissue and bone overgrowth, or various syndromes, including Sturge-Weber syndrome, Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome, Parkes-Weber syndrome, Servelle-Martorell syndrome, Proteus syndrome, CLOVES syndrome, Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome, capillary malformation-arteriovenous malformation syndrome, macrocephaly-capillary malformation syndrome, microcephaly-capillary malformation syndrome, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history and examination. Newborn screening for other congenital and genetic anomalies may be indicated, including urgent ophthalmology review and brain MRI. Pulsed dye laser (PDL) treatment is considered the gold standard for managing port-wine stains. Surgery may be considered if the lesion is associated with bone and soft tissue overgrowth. Reticulate Capillary Malformations Reticulate capillary malformations are widespread vascular anomalies presenting as numerous oval or circular macules or patches, ranging in size from a few millimeters to several centimeters. These lesions are associated with two syndromes: CM of MIC-CAP (microcephaly-capillary malformation) CM of MCAP (megalencephaly-capillary malformation-polymicrogyria) Capillary Malformations of CM-AVM These malformations are typically multiple, round to oval, and range in color from pink-red to tan. They are found in patches measuring 1 to 2 cm in size and are scattered throughout the body. New lesions may continue to appear during childhood. In some cases, a high-flow murmur can be detected using a Doppler device. These malformations are associated with capillary malformation-arteriovenous malformation syndrome, an autosomal dominant condition linked to mutations in the RASA1 gene. Cutis Marmorata Telangiectatica Congenita (CMTC) CMTC is a congenital vascular malformation involving capillary and venous-sized vessels. It presents as fixed reticulate erythema, similar to physiologic cutis marmorata, but does not resolve with warming. It may be associated with skin ulceration, atrophy, and undergrowth of the affected extremity. Findings may include prominent veins, telangiectasias, cutaneous atrophy, ulceration, and hyperkeratosis. The lesions may be localized or generalized. In localized patterns, the lesions are confined to one side of the body and do not cross the midline, with or without sharp demarcation. CMTC may be associated with other abnormalities, the most common being limb asymmetry. Other associated findings include glaucoma, port-wine stains, angiokeratomas, and hemangiomas. It may also be linked to Sturge-Weber syndrome. Most cases are sporadic, but an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern has been observed in familial cases. Diagnosis is clinical, based on history and examination. Management depends on systemic involvement, and skin lesions often improve spontaneously. Telangiectasia Telangiectasia refers to the permanent dilation of preexisting blood vessels, resulting in small focal red lesions, most commonly in the skin or mucous membranes. It is characterized by the prominence of skin blood vessels, such as vascular spiders. For more information on hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), further resources are available.
